questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: A 61-year-old woman reports leaking urine several times a day for the past year. Her history includes type 2 diabetes, a BMI of 34, smoking one pack a day, chronic constipation, and furosemide 40 mg every morning for hypertension. She drinks about 2,200 mL of water spread through the day and eats a high-fiber cereal each morning. Which factors in her history increase her risk for urinary incontinence? Select all that apply.
options: Daily furosemide
BMI of 34
Drinking about 2,200 mL of water spread through the day
Type 2 diabetes
Eating a high-fiber cereal each morning
Chronic constipation
optionRationales: Correct. Diuretics fill the bladder faster. A fast rise in volume raises bladder pressure until it can exceed urethral pressure, and urine escapes.
Correct. Obesity adds steady abdominal pressure on the bladder and pelvic floor. This raises bladder pressure and weakens urethral support.
This is protective. Fluids should not be limited. More than 2,000 mL a day, spaced out, keeps urine dilute so it does not irritate the bladder wall.
Correct. Diabetes is a listed risk factor for urinary incontinence. It can damage the nerves that signal and control the bladder, and high glucose increases urine volume.
This is protective. A high-fiber diet prevents constipation, and constipation is itself a risk factor for incontinence.
Correct. A rectum full of hard stool presses on the bladder and urethra and strains the pelvic floor. Constipation is a listed risk factor.
questions.rationale: Incontinence happens when bladder pressure exceeds urethral pressure. Anything that adds volume (diuretics, high glucose), adds pressure (obesity, constipation), or damages control (diabetic nerve damage) raises risk. Smoking is also on her list. Adequate fluid spaced through the day and a high-fiber diet are prevention measures, not risks.
questions.takeaway: Risk = more volume, more pressure, or less control. Adequate fluids and fiber protect the bladder.
questions.hintContent: Connect the pressure explanation of incontinence (bladder vs. urethra) to medications, body weight, bowel habits, and chronic disease. Recall the lifestyle measures that prevent incontinence.
questions.hintStrategy: Judge each item on its own. Ask whether it adds bladder volume or pressure, weakens control, or is a recommended prevention habit.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old client gave birth to her third child 4 months ago. She tells the nurse, “I leak a little whenever I laugh, sneeze, or pick up my toddler. I don’t feel any urge before it happens, and I only get up once a night to void.” Which explanation best fits her symptoms?
options: Childbirth weakened her pelvic floor and urethra, so sudden abdominal pressure overcomes urethral resistance
An overactive detrusor muscle contracts before the bladder is full, so she cannot delay voiding once the contraction starts
A blockage at the bladder outlet lets the bladder overfill, and urine spills out when the pressure gets high enough
Nerve damage from delivery causes detrusor spasms, so the bladder empties without any warning sensation
optionRationales: Correct. This is stress incontinence. Pregnancy and delivery weaken the pelvic floor and urethra, so laughing, sneezing, or lifting raises bladder pressure above urethral resistance.
This describes urge incontinence. Urge incontinence brings a strong urge and often nocturia, and she reports neither.
This describes overflow incontinence from outlet obstruction or a weak detrusor. It causes ongoing leaking from an overfull bladder, not leaking only with exertion.
This describes reflex incontinence. Reflex incontinence comes from neurologic impairment such as MS or spinal cord injury, not from routine childbirth.
questions.rationale: Stress incontinence comes from relaxed pelvic muscles and a weak urethra, which lower urethral resistance. Pregnancy and delivery are classic causes. Small leaks triggered by coughing, sneezing, laughing, or lifting are the hallmark. One void a night is not a sign of urge incontinence.
questions.takeaway: Leaking with a cough, sneeze, laugh, or lift and no urge = stress incontinence (weak urethral resistance).
questions.hintContent: Recall the five types of urinary incontinence and the trigger and cause of each. Consider what pregnancy and delivery do to the pelvic floor.
questions.hintStrategy: Find the trigger (exertion, urge, no sensation, or overfilling). Then pick the mechanism that matches that trigger.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old man with benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) reports constant dribbling for the past month. He describes a weak stream, a feeling that his bladder never empties, and two urinary tract infections this year. His lower abdomen is slightly rounded above the pubis. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Teach him Kegel exercises to strengthen the pelvic floor muscles
Perform a bladder scan after he voids to measure the residual urine
Start a bladder-training schedule to gradually lengthen the time between voids
Provide absorbent undergarments to protect his skin from the dribbling
optionRationales: Kegels treat stress and urge incontinence. They do not relieve an outlet blocked by an enlarged prostate.

Correct. These cues suggest overflow incontinence: a blocked outlet causes retention and leakage. Measuring the post-void residual confirms how much urine is retained, and that guides catheterization and the provider’s plan.
Making him wait longer between voids would let an already overfull bladder fill even more. Bladder training is used for urge incontinence.
Protecting his skin matters, but it treats only the symptom. It does not address the retained urine causing the dribbling and the infections.
questions.rationale: BPH, a weak stream, a feeling of incomplete emptying, constant dribbling, repeated UTIs, and a suprapubic bulge all point to overflow incontinence. An obstructed outlet lets the bladder overfill until urine leaks out. The first step is to measure the retained volume. Therapies for other types, such as Kegels and bladder training, will not help and can make retention worse.
questions.takeaway: Dribbling plus a feeling of incomplete emptying in a man with BPH = think overflow. Measure the residual first.
questions.hintContent: Connect BPH, a weak stream, incomplete emptying, and UTIs to a type of incontinence. Recall how retained urine is measured.
questions.hintStrategy: Name the incontinence type first. Then choose the action that assesses the underlying problem before you treat it.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A client with a T6 spinal cord injury from a fall 2 years ago is being assessed for incontinence. Which statement by the client is most consistent with reflex incontinence?
options: “I leak a little whenever I cough hard or someone helps me transfer.”
“I get a sudden, strong urge, and I can’t hold it long enough to get there.”
“I’ll suddenly notice I’m wet, and I never felt I needed to go at all.”
“By the time I get my chair lined up next to the toilet, I’ve already started to go.”
optionRationales: Leaking with coughing or physical strain describes stress incontinence.
A strong urge with inability to delay describes urge incontinence. In reflex incontinence the client feels no urge.
Correct. Neurologic damage such as spinal cord injury causes detrusor spasms, so the bladder empties suddenly with no sensation of needing to void.
Being unable to reach the toilet in time because of mobility limits describes functional incontinence.
questions.rationale: In reflex incontinence, damage to nerve pathways (spinal cord injury, MS) causes detrusor spasms. The bladder empties without the person sensing fullness, which is the neurogenic bladder pattern. The key cue is urination without any urge.
questions.takeaway: Reflex incontinence = neurologic damage plus voiding with NO urge.
questions.hintContent: Recall what a spinal cord injury does to the sensation and control of bladder emptying (neurogenic bladder).
questions.hintStrategy: Match each quote to a type by its trigger: exertion, urge, mobility barrier, or no sensation.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
questions.stem: An 84-year-old long-term care resident with moderate dementia walks with a walker. She is continent when staff take her to the bathroom but is often found wet in the hallway. She wears pants with a button and zipper. Which interventions are appropriate for her type of incontinence? Select all that apply.
options: Offer toileting assistance at regular, scheduled intervals
Replace button-and-zipper pants with elastic-waist pants
Request a prescription for an anticholinergic to relax the detrusor muscle
Place a bedside commode and raised toilet seat to shorten the trip
Limit her fluids after lunch so her bladder fills less often
Request a physical therapy referral to improve her transfers and walking
optionRationales: Correct. Scheduled toileting gets her to the bathroom before urgency. She cannot reliably recognize and act on the need herself.
Correct. Nonrestrictive clothing removes a barrier. Fumbling with buttons and zippers costs time she does not have.
Her bladder works normally. The problem is reaching the toilet. Anticholinergics treat an overactive detrusor and can add confusion and retention in older adults.
Correct. Assistive devices and environmental changes shorten the distance and effort needed to reach a toilet.
Fluids should not be limited during the day. Low intake concentrates urine, which irritates the bladder. Only nighttime fluids are reduced.
Correct. PT/OT is listed therapy for functional incontinence. Better mobility helps her reach the toilet in time.
questions.rationale: This is functional incontinence. Her bladder works, but dementia and impaired mobility slow her response to the urge to void. Treatment removes barriers: scheduled toileting, nonrestrictive clothing, assistive devices, home or environmental changes, and PT/OT. Drugs that target the bladder and daytime fluid limits do not address the cause.
questions.takeaway: Functional incontinence: the bladder is fine, the trip to the toilet is the problem. Remove the barriers.
questions.hintContent: Identify the type of incontinence from the cues (continent when assisted, dementia, walker). Then recall the therapies for that type.
questions.hintStrategy: For each option, ask: does this make it easier to reach the toilet in time, or does it treat a bladder problem she doesn’t have?

questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: A 56-year-old postmenopausal client asks the nurse why she has started leaking urine since menopause. Which explanation by the nurse is accurate?
options: “Leaking urine is an expected part of aging that usually begins around menopause.”
“After menopause, your kidneys make more urine at night, and that overfills the bladder.”
“Menopause causes the bladder muscle to lose its nerve supply, so it empties on its own without warning.”
“Lower estrogen thins the tissues that help hold the urethra closed, so urine escapes more easily.”
optionRationales: Incontinence is never a normal consequence of aging. It is a symptom with a cause, and treatment options exist.
This does not explain menopause-related leaking. Nighttime urine production changes with kidney aging and is not the cause given here.
Loss of nerve control describes reflex incontinence from conditions such as MS or spinal cord injury. Menopause does not cause it.
Correct. Decreased estrogen during menopause is a listed cause. Thinner, weaker urethral and pelvic tissue lowers urethral resistance, so bladder pressure overcomes it more easily.
questions.rationale: Incontinence happens when bladder pressure exceeds urethral pressure. Low estrogen after menopause weakens the urethral and pelvic tissues that provide resistance. That is why topical estrogen is a therapy for some postmenopausal women. Incontinence is a symptom, not a normal part of aging.
questions.takeaway: Low estrogen means weaker urethral tissue and less resistance. Incontinence is never "just aging."
questions.hintContent: Recall the three causes listed for increased bladder pressure or decreased resistance (diuretics, pregnancy, decreased estrogen). Recall whether incontinence is a normal part of aging.
questions.hintStrategy: Eliminate any statement that normalizes incontinence. Then choose the mechanism that links estrogen to urethral resistance.

questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care
questions.stem: A nurse in a long-term care facility receives reports on four residents with urinary incontinence. Which resident should the nurse assess first?
options: A resident with BPH who has had only small dribbles all shift and is now restless, with lower abdominal fullness
A resident with long-standing stress incontinence who is leaking more often with each coughing spell during a cold
A resident with dementia and functional incontinence who was found wet at 0300 for the second night in a row
A resident with multiple sclerosis and reflex incontinence who is asking for a clean brief
optionRationales: Correct. Dribbling, restlessness, and lower abdominal fullness in a man with BPH suggest the bladder is overdistended with retained urine. Acute retention is a medical emergency, so this resident is seen first.
Coughing raises abdominal pressure, so more leaking is an expected worsening of known stress incontinence. It is not an emergency.
Nighttime episodes call for a toileting plan, but this is a stable, expected pattern for functional incontinence.
This resident needs hygiene and skin care soon. A wet brief with known reflex incontinence is expected and stable.
questions.rationale: The resident with BPH is showing overflow from an obstructed, overdistended bladder, which can become painful acute retention. Acute retention is a medical emergency, and the bladder may need decompression. The other residents have expected patterns of known incontinence that need routine care.
questions.takeaway: Dribbling, restlessness, and a full lower abdomen = possible retention. Retention outranks routine incontinence care.
questions.hintContent: Compare expected, stable incontinence patterns with signs of an overdistended bladder. Recall which form of retention is an emergency.
questions.hintStrategy: Ask which resident has a new change that could cause harm if not addressed. The rest have expected findings for their known type.

questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: A nurse teaches a community group of older adults how to prevent urinary incontinence. Which statements by participants indicate understanding? Select all that apply.
options: “I’ll drink at least 2 liters of fluid a day, spread out, and cut back in the evening.”
“I’ll switch from regular soda to diet soda to be easier on my bladder.”
“If I drink less water during the day, my bladder will be less irritated.”
“Losing some weight could take pressure off my bladder.”
“Quitting smoking may help keep me from developing leaking.”
optionRationales: Correct. More than 2,000 mL a day, spaced throughout the day and limited at night, prevents concentrated urine and nocturia.
Artificial sweeteners are bladder irritants. Diet soda can also contain caffeine.
Less intake makes urine more concentrated, and concentrated urine irritates the bladder wall. Daytime fluids should not be limited.
Correct. Keeping a healthy weight lowers abdominal pressure on the bladder. It is a key lifestyle change.
Correct. Smoking is a risk factor, and stopping smoking is a recommended lifestyle change.
questions.rationale: Lifestyle prevention includes a healthy weight, exercise, stopping smoking, a high-fiber diet, avoiding bladder irritants (alcohol, caffeine, artificial sweeteners, acidic or spicy foods), and adequate fluid. Adequate fluid means more than 2,000 mL a day, spaced out and limited at night. Limiting fluid concentrates urine and irritates the bladder.
questions.takeaway: Don’t limit daytime fluids: low intake means concentrated urine, which irritates the bladder. Avoid irritants, including artificial sweeteners.
questions.hintContent: Recall the lifestyle changes that prevent incontinence, the bladder-irritant list, and the fluid recommendation.
questions.hintStrategy: Check each statement against the prevention list. Watch for swaps that sound healthy but add an irritant, and for fluid limits.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old client with heart failure started furosemide 40 mg every morning last week. She now reports a sudden, strong need to void and small leaks during the late morning, which she never had before. Her weight is down 1.5 kg, and her edema is improving. Which recommendation by the nurse is best?
options: “Take the furosemide at bedtime instead, so the extra urine comes while you’re resting in bed.”
“Keep the morning dose and plan to be near a bathroom for the few hours after you take it.”
“Limit your fluids to about 1 liter a day so the medicine doesn’t make as much urine.”
“Skip the dose on days you plan to be away from home until the leaking stops.”
optionRationales: A bedtime dose would cause nocturia, interrupt sleep, and raise fall risk on nighttime trips to the bathroom.
Correct. The diuretic is working. It quickly increases bladder volume and pressure, so planning for easy bathroom access after the dose prevents leaks safely.
Restricting fluids concentrates urine, which irritates the bladder. Fluid changes for heart failure are the provider’s decision, not a fix for leaking.
Skipping doses risks worsening heart failure. The nurse should not advise stopping a prescribed drug.
questions.rationale: Diuretics are a listed cause of incontinence. They raise bladder volume quickly, and bladder pressure can then exceed urethral pressure. Her weight loss and improving edema show the drug is working. The safest approach keeps the morning timing and plans toileting around the expected diuresis. Bedtime dosing, fluid limits, or skipped doses each create a new problem.
questions.takeaway: Diuretic-related urgency: keep the dose in the morning and plan bathroom access. Don’t limit fluids or skip doses.
questions.hintContent: Connect how diuretics raise bladder volume to the timing of urgency. Recall why fluids shouldn’t be limited and why nocturia is avoided.
questions.hintStrategy: Each wrong option fixes the leaking but creates a new safety problem. Find the one that keeps the therapy and prevents leaks.

questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
questions.stem: An 82-year-old client who was continent at home has had three incontinence episodes since being admitted for pneumonia. Which factors in the hospital setting may be contributing? Select all that apply.
options: The call light was clipped to the far side rail, out of reach
Her eyeglasses were left at home
She shares a semiprivate room separated only by a curtain
She is drinking about 2,000 mL of fluid spread through the day
An IV pole and tubing make it hard for her to get up quickly
Her bed is in the lowest position, and she wears nonslip socks
optionRationales: Correct. Without a way to call for help, she has no assistance and loses time getting to the toilet.
Correct. Impaired vision makes it harder to find and reach the bathroom safely in an unfamiliar room.
Correct. Lack of privacy can make older adults delay voiding until they leak.
This is adequate, appropriately spaced intake. It is not a cause of incontinence.
Correct. Equipment limits her mobility and slows her response to the urge to void.
These are fall-prevention measures. They make getting up safer and do not contribute to incontinence.
questions.rationale: Older adults are at risk for incontinence from limited mobility, impaired vision, dementia, lack of access to toilets, no assistance, and lack of privacy. A hospital adds new barriers: an unreachable call light, missing glasses, shared rooms, and IV equipment. Fixing these barriers is often enough to restore continence.
questions.takeaway: New incontinence in a hospitalized older adult? Look for barriers: mobility, vision, assistance, access, privacy.
questions.hintContent: Recall the lifespan factors that contribute to incontinence in older adults.
questions.hintStrategy: For each item, ask whether it slows or blocks her from getting to the toilet, or whether it is a protective measure.

questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: The parent of an 8-year-old reports, “He was dry at night for over a year, but since we moved and he started a new school 2 months ago, he’s been wetting the bed most nights.” Which response by the nurse is most accurate?
options: “Bedwetting is expected until about age 10, so no evaluation is needed for now.”
“Because this started suddenly, a kidney or bladder disease is the most likely cause.”
“This is secondary enuresis, and finding out what changed is key to helping him.”
“He has primary enuresis, which almost always goes away once he sleeps more lightly.”
optionRationales: Nighttime enuresis is not considered a problem until after age 7. At 8, with new loss of control, he needs evaluation.
Most often enuresis is not caused by a medical disorder. Stress such as a move or a new school is a common trigger.
Correct. Losing nighttime control after at least 6 months of dryness is secondary enuresis. Understanding why it started is essential to the child’s outcome and well-being.
Primary enuresis means the child has never had nighttime control. This child was dry for more than 6 months.
questions.rationale: Primary enuresis means the child has never had nighttime control. Secondary enuresis means control lasted at least 6 months and was then lost. Understanding the cause is essential, and most enuresis is not due to a medical disorder. Life stressors such as a move are common triggers. Nighttime wetting is not considered a problem until after age 7.
questions.takeaway: Dry 6 months or more, then wetting again = secondary enuresis. Find out why.
questions.hintContent: Recall the definitions of primary and secondary enuresis, the age when nighttime wetting becomes a concern, and the usual causes.
questions.hintStrategy: Classify the enuresis from the history first. Then rule out options that misstate the age cutoff or the usual cause.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: A 66-year-old client with urge incontinence is scheduled to begin bladder training today. She tells the nurse that for the past 2 days the urgency has been much worse, voiding burns, and her urine is cloudy and foul-smelling. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Begin the bladder-training schedule today to lengthen the time between her voids
Teach her to do Kegel exercises when she feels the urge to void
Suggest that she drink less fluid until the urgency improves
Obtain a urine specimen as prescribed and report her symptoms
optionRationales: Bladder training is appropriate for urge incontinence, but it should not start while a possible infection is causing the urgency.
Kegels help suppress urgency. They are not the first step when new symptoms point to an infection.
Limiting fluids concentrates urine and irritates the bladder further. Adequate fluid is encouraged.
Correct. Dysuria and cloudy, foul-smelling urine suggest a UTI, a listed risk factor that worsens incontinence. A urinalysis and culture identify the infection so it can be treated first.
questions.rationale: New, worse urgency with dysuria and cloudy, foul-smelling urine suggests a UTI. UTI is a risk factor for incontinence, and medication for UTI is part of incontinence therapy. Treating the underlying cause comes before starting behavior therapy. Otherwise training is set up to fail, and the infection goes untreated.
questions.takeaway: Sudden worse urgency with burning and cloudy urine: check for UTI before starting bladder training.
questions.hintContent: Connect UTI as a risk factor for incontinence with the diagnostic tests for urine and the therapies for incontinence.
questions.hintStrategy: When symptoms suddenly change, look for a treatable cause before starting long-term behavior therapy.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Exemplar: Bladder Incontinence & Retention · Managing Urinary Incontinence: Kegels, Bladder Training, Devices & Meds
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: A nurse teaches Kegel exercises to a client who is 24 weeks pregnant and has started leaking urine when she sneezes. Which statements by the client indicate understanding? Select all that apply.
options: “I’ll squeeze the same muscles I’d use to stop my urine stream or hold back a bowel movement.”
“I’ll hold each squeeze for 3 to 10 seconds.”
“I’ll tighten my stomach and buttock muscles too, so the squeeze is stronger.”
“I’ll relax for 10 to 15 seconds between squeezes and repeat about 10 times.”
“I should wait until after the baby is born to start these exercises.”
“I’ll hold my breath during each squeeze to help me focus.”
optionRationales: Correct. Stopping the urine flow and resisting a bowel movement are how the client identifies the pelvic floor muscles.
Correct. Each contraction is held for 3 to 10 seconds.
Kegels isolate the pelvic floor. Tightening the abdominal and buttock muscles raises abdominal pressure and does not train the right muscles.
Correct. She relaxes for 10 to 15 seconds between contractions and repeats the set 10 times.
Kegels are recommended during pregnancy to counter the weight of the uterus and hormonal changes on the pelvic floor.
Holding the breath bears down and raises abdominal pressure. She should breathe normally.
questions.rationale: Kegel exercises strengthen the pelvic floor, improving perineal muscle tone for the bladder and rectum. The client finds the muscles by stopping urine flow or resisting a bowel movement. She holds 3 to 10 seconds, relaxes 10 to 15 seconds, and repeats 10 times. Kegels are encouraged during pregnancy, when hormones and the growing uterus strain the pelvic floor and cause stress incontinence.
questions.takeaway: Kegels: find the muscle, hold 3–10 sec, relax 10–15 sec, repeat ×10. Start during pregnancy.
questions.hintContent: Recall the steps for teaching Kegel exercises and the pregnancy-related causes of stress incontinence.
questions.hintStrategy: Check each statement against the Kegel steps. Reject anything that adds abdominal pressure or delays starting.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Exemplar: Bladder Incontinence & Retention · Managing Urinary Incontinence: Kegels, Bladder Training, Devices & Meds
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
questions.stem: A cognitively intact 59-year-old client with urge incontinence voids about every hour and has two or three leaks a day. The provider orders bladder training. Which instruction should the nurse give first?
options: “Write down each void, its amount, and any leaks in a bladder diary for a few days.”
“Start waiting a full 4 hours between trips to the bathroom, beginning with today’s schedule.”
“Do a quick Kegel squeeze to calm the urge whenever you need to wait.”
“Cut back to about 1,000 mL of fluid a day so your bladder fills more slowly.”
optionRationales: Correct. A bladder diary sets the baseline pattern. The voiding schedule is built from it and then gradually lengthened.
The goal interval is 3 to 4 hours, but intervals are lengthened gradually from her current baseline. Jumping to 4 hours would cause more leaks and discouragement.
Kegels to suppress the urge are part of bladder training, but they come once the schedule is set. Without a baseline, there is no schedule yet.
Limiting fluids concentrates urine, which irritates the bladder and worsens urgency.
questions.rationale: Bladder training lengthens the interval between voids toward 3 to 4 hours to reduce frequency and urgency and stabilize the bladder. Kegels are used to inhibit the urge in between. It starts with a bladder diary, because the schedule is built from her actual pattern and lengthened gradually. Fluid restriction works against the goal.
questions.takeaway: Bladder training starts with a diary, then the interval is lengthened gradually toward 3–4 hours, with Kegels to hold off the urge.
questions.hintContent: Recall the components of bladder training: diary, schedule, gradual lengthening, and urge inhibition.
questions.hintStrategy: Several options are parts of bladder training. Ask which one has to come before the others can work.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.stem: A client with urge incontinence has a new prescription for oxybutynin (Ditropan). Before giving the first dose, which finding in the client’s record is most important for the nurse to report to the provider?
options: Nocturia three times a night
Glaucoma treated with daily eye drops
Topical vaginal estrogen applied twice weekly
Two cups of caffeinated coffee each morning
optionRationales: Nocturia is a manifestation of urge incontinence, one of the problems oxybutynin is meant to treat.
Correct. Anticholinergics such as oxybutynin should be avoided in clients with glaucoma because they can raise eye pressure.
Topical estrogen is another therapy for incontinence in postmenopausal women. It is not a reason to hold the anticholinergic.
Caffeine is a bladder irritant to address in teaching, but it is not a safety concern that requires holding the drug.
questions.rationale: Anticholinergics such as oxybutynin relax the overactive detrusor muscle to reduce urgency and frequency. They have significant side effects and should be avoided in clients with glaucoma. The other findings are related to incontinence and call for teaching, not for questioning the prescription.
questions.takeaway: Oxybutynin (anticholinergic): avoid in glaucoma.
questions.hintContent: Recall the anticholinergic used for urge incontinence, how it works, and the condition in which it should be avoided.
questions.hintStrategy: Separate findings that are part of the problem being treated from findings that make the drug unsafe.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.stem: A 72-year-old man with BPH and overflow incontinence starts a smooth-muscle relaxant to improve urine flow. Which teaching points should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: “Change positions slowly, from lying to sitting to standing.”
“Tell your provider if you feel dizzy or lightheaded.”
“Your stream may get weaker for the first few weeks before it improves.”
“Your blood pressure may be checked lying down and standing.”
“Drink no more than 1 liter a day so your bladder doesn’t overfill.”
optionRationales: Correct. Smooth-muscle relaxants used for BPH can lower blood pressure. Rising slowly prevents falls from orthostatic drops.
Correct. Dizziness can signal low blood pressure and should be reported.
The drug relaxes smooth muscle at the bladder outlet to improve flow. A weaker stream would suggest the drug isn’t working and should not be expected.
Correct. Monitoring for decreased blood pressure is the key nursing focus with these drugs.
Fluid restriction concentrates urine, irritates the bladder, and raises UTI risk. More than 2,000 mL a day is recommended.
questions.rationale: For BPH, smooth-muscle relaxants ease outlet obstruction so the bladder can empty. The main monitoring point is decreased blood pressure, so teaching centers on rising slowly, reporting dizziness, and checking BP. Fluid restriction is not part of incontinence or retention management.
questions.takeaway: BPH smooth-muscle relaxants: watch for low BP. Rise slowly and report dizziness.
questions.hintContent: Recall the medication therapy listed for BPH and the monitoring point that goes with it.
questions.hintStrategy: Choose options that relate to the drug’s known risk. Reject expectations that contradict what the drug is supposed to do.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old postmenopausal client with atrophic vaginitis and stress incontinence is prescribed a topical vaginal estrogen cream. She asks how a cream will help her leaking. Which explanation by the nurse is accurate?
options: “It relaxes the bladder muscle so it doesn’t squeeze before your bladder is full.”
“It treats the bacteria that cause bladder infections, which then reduces your leaking.”
“It helps rebuild thin urethral and vaginal tissue so the urethra closes better.”
“It makes your kidneys produce less urine, so the bladder fills more slowly.”
optionRationales: Relaxing the detrusor muscle is the action of anticholinergics used for urge incontinence.
Antibiotics treat UTIs. Estrogen is not an antibiotic.
Correct. Low estrogen after menopause thins the urethral and vaginal tissue and lowers urethral resistance. Topical estrogen restores that tissue.
Estrogen does not reduce urine production. Lowering bladder volume is not how it helps.
questions.rationale: Decreased estrogen during menopause is a listed cause of incontinence, because thinner tissue means less urethral resistance. Topical estrogen is used for postmenopausal women with atrophic vaginitis. It restores tissue tone so the urethra resists bladder pressure better. This is different from how anticholinergics or antibiotics work.
questions.takeaway: Topical estrogen rebuilds thin postmenopausal tissue, which increases urethral resistance.
questions.hintContent: Connect the cause (low estrogen means weak urethral tissue) to the therapy (topical estrogen).
questions.hintStrategy: Match the drug to its mechanism. Eliminate options that describe a different drug class.

questions.stem: The parents of a 9-year-old with primary nocturnal enuresis say they have tried limiting drinks after dinner, with little improvement. A medical cause has been ruled out. Which treatment should the nurse explain is most effective for bedwetting?
options: Waking the child every 2 hours through the night to void
Stopping all fluids after school each day
Medication, because it is the first and most effective treatment
A bedwetting alarm that wakes the child when wetting begins
optionRationales: Waking a child on a fixed schedule disrupts sleep and does not teach the child to respond to bladder signals.
Stopping fluids for that long risks dehydration and concentrated urine, and it does not address the cause.
Medications are sometimes used, but alarms are the most effective treatment. Behavioral and dietary changes come first.
Correct. Alarms are the most effective treatment for bedwetting. They condition the child to wake to the sensation of a full bladder.
questions.rationale: Enuresis is treated with behavioral changes, dietary changes to manage constipation, and sometimes medication. Bedwetting alarms are the most effective treatment. Most nighttime enuresis improves as the child matures.
questions.takeaway: The most effective treatment for bedwetting is an alarm.
questions.hintContent: Recall the key points about enuresis treatment, especially which treatment is described as most effective.
questions.hintStrategy: Several options sound active. Pick the one the evidence names as most effective, not the most restrictive one.

questions.stem: A resident with moderate dementia and functional incontinence has a 3-day bladder diary showing that she usually voids soon after waking, after each meal, and at about 1500 and 2100. The care plan calls for habit training. Which instruction to the assistive personnel is most important?
options: “Take her to the bathroom at the times her diary shows she usually voids.”
“Remind her to do her pelvic floor squeezes every hour while she is awake.”
“Check her brief every 4 hours and change it promptly if it is wet.”
“Hold her fluids after supper so she stays dry through the night.”
optionRationales: Correct. Habit training means voiding at the times identified in the bladder diary to prevent incontinence episodes.
Kegels require the client to understand and cooperate. They do not fit moderate dementia, and they are not habit training.
Checking and changing the brief protects the skin but only contains the incontinence. It does not prevent episodes.
Fluids are limited only near bedtime to prevent nocturia, not cut off after supper. Restriction concentrates urine.
questions.rationale: Habit training uses the bladder diary to time voiding to the client’s own pattern and prevent incontinence episodes. It suits clients with cognitive impairment who cannot follow bladder training. Brief changes and skin care are needed, but they do not prevent episodes.
questions.takeaway: Habit training = toilet at the client’s own diary-identified times.
questions.hintContent: Distinguish bladder training, habit training, and scheduled toileting. Consider which fits a client with dementia.
questions.hintStrategy: Choose the instruction that carries out the ordered therapy and prevents episodes, rather than only managing them.

questions.stem: A nurse reviews the plans of care for several clients with incontinence. Which device or therapy is appropriately matched to the client? Select all that apply.
options: A pessary for a woman with stress incontinence related to a cystocele
Intermittent catheterization for a client with a neurogenic bladder who retains urine
An indwelling catheter for an alert, mobile client with urge incontinence, to keep her dry
A urethral insert for a man with BPH and dribbling
An anticholinergic for a man with overflow incontinence from BPH
Absorbent undergarments and nonrestrictive clothing for a client with functional incontinence
optionRationales: Correct. A pessary is inserted to support a prolapsed bladder and is a listed therapy for stress incontinence in women.

Correct. Catheterization is indicated for overflow from retention or a neurogenic bladder. Intermittent ‘in and out’ catheterization empties the bladder with less infection risk than an indwelling catheter.
Indwelling catheters carry a high UTI risk. For urge incontinence, behavior therapy and medications come first, so the risk outweighs the benefit here.
Pessaries and urethral inserts are devices for women.
Anticholinergics are a known risk factor for urinary retention. They would worsen overflow from an obstructed outlet.
Correct. Absorbent undergarments and nonrestrictive clothing are listed therapies for functional incontinence.
questions.rationale: Each therapy has to fit the mechanism. Devices for women (pessary, urethral insert) support the bladder and urethra in stress incontinence. Catheterization is for overflow from retention or a neurogenic bladder, with risk weighed against benefit. Anticholinergics treat urge incontinence but cause retention, so they are wrong for overflow from BPH.
questions.takeaway: Match the therapy to the mechanism. Anticholinergics worsen retention, and catheters are for retention, not convenience.
questions.hintContent: Recall the devices and medications for each incontinence type and the risk-benefit view of catheters.
questions.hintStrategy: For each pairing, ask whether the therapy fixes this client’s mechanism or makes it worse.

questions.stem: Six weeks into bladder training for urge incontinence, a client’s diary shows that the time between voids has increased from 1 hour to 2½ hours. She has had no leaks for 4 days and still gets up once a night to void. How should the nurse evaluate her progress?
options: The therapy is not working because she still has nocturia, so an anticholinergic should be added
She is progressing, so the interval should keep lengthening gradually toward 3 to 4 hours
The goal has been met, so she can stop the diary and the schedule
She should stop all fluids after 1800 to get rid of the remaining night-time voiding
optionRationales: Getting up once a night is not a reason to call training a failure. Her daytime pattern shows clear improvement.
Correct. A longer interval and no leaks show progress toward the 3- to 4-hour goal, so training continues with gradual lengthening.
The target interval is 3 to 4 hours. Stopping at 2½ hours leaves the goal unmet.
Fluids are limited at night, not stopped early in the evening. Restriction concentrates urine and irritates the bladder.
questions.rationale: Bladder training gradually lengthens the voiding interval to 3 to 4 hours to stabilize the bladder and reduce urgency. Going from 1 hour to 2½ hours with no leaks is clear progress, but the goal is not yet met. Evaluation compares the data to the goal, then continues the plan or explores obstacles before changing it.
questions.takeaway: Evaluate against the goal (a 3–4 hour interval). Progress means continue, not stop or switch.
questions.hintContent: Recall the target interval for bladder training and how to evaluate progress toward a goal.
questions.hintStrategy: Compare her current numbers to the stated goal. Is she there, partway, or getting worse?

questions.stem: An 81-year-old client started oxybutynin 4 days ago for urge incontinence. Today she is restless and newly confused, has not voided in 8 hours despite normal intake, and reports lower abdominal discomfort. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Hold the next dose of oxybutynin and document the confusion
Encourage her to drink 500 mL of fluid to stimulate voiding
Palpate and percuss the lower abdomen and perform a bladder scan
Insert an indwelling urinary catheter to drain her bladder completely
optionRationales: Holding the next dose and reporting it is appropriate, but it comes after confirming retention. It does not address urine that may already be retained.
Adding fluid to a bladder that cannot empty increases distention and discomfort.
Correct. Anticholinergics are a risk factor for urinary retention. Assessing for a firm, distended bladder with dullness and measuring the volume confirms retention and guides the next step.
Catheterization may be needed, but it requires an order and should follow an assessment that confirms retention.
questions.rationale: Anticholinergics reduce detrusor contraction, which helps urge incontinence but can cause urinary retention. In an older adult they can also cause confusion. No voiding for 8 hours, restlessness, and lower abdominal discomfort suggest retention. Assessment comes first: palpate and percuss for a firm, dull bladder, then scan to measure the volume.
questions.takeaway: Anticholinergic plus no voiding plus discomfort = suspect retention. Assess and scan the bladder first.
questions.hintContent: Connect the action of anticholinergics to urinary retention. Recall the physical findings and the test that confirm a full bladder.
questions.hintStrategy: Several options are reasonable steps. Ask which one confirms the suspected problem before you act on it.

questions.stem: A client at 30 weeks’ gestation reports small leaks when she coughs or lifts her toddler. Which statements should the nurse include in teaching? Select all that apply.
options: “Doing Kegel exercises now can strengthen the muscles that support your bladder.”
“The weight of your growing uterus and hormone changes can cause this leaking.”
“Drink less than 1 liter a day until the baby is born to reduce leaking.”
“Leaking during pregnancy means there is permanent damage that will need surgery.”
“Cutting back on caffeine and artificial sweeteners can make your bladder less irritable.”
optionRationales: Correct. Kegel exercises are recommended during pregnancy to improve pelvic floor tone.
Correct. Hormonal changes and the weight of the growing uterus raise bladder pressure and weaken support, a classic cause of stress incontinence.
Limiting fluids concentrates urine and irritates the bladder. Pregnant clients especially need adequate fluid.
Pregnancy-related leaking often improves with pelvic floor exercises. Trauma or prolapse after delivery can contribute, but surgery is not the expected outcome.
Correct. Avoiding bladder irritants such as caffeine and artificial sweeteners is part of lifestyle modification.
questions.rationale: In pregnancy, hormones and the weight of the uterus raise bladder pressure and weaken pelvic support, which causes stress incontinence. Teaching includes Kegel exercises during pregnancy, avoiding bladder irritants, and keeping fluid intake adequate.
questions.takeaway: Pregnancy leaking: Kegels now, avoid irritants, and don’t limit fluids.
questions.hintContent: Recall the pregnancy-related causes of incontinence and the lifestyle and exercise therapies.
questions.hintStrategy: Keep options that are accurate and protective. Reject fluid restriction and statements that overstate the prognosis.

questions.stem: A client is 6 hours post-op after a hip repair under spinal anesthesia and has not voided since surgery. The client is restless and reports severe lower abdominal pain and a strong urge but cannot void. The nurse palpates a firm, distended bladder above the pubis, and percussion is dull. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Give the prescribed PRN opioid for the abdominal pain
Encourage 500 mL of oral fluids to help start a stream
Document the findings and recheck in 1 hour
Perform a bladder scan to measure the volume of urine
optionRationales: Opioids do not relieve a distended bladder and can worsen retention. The pain is a cue to find and treat the cause.
More fluid would add to a bladder that already cannot empty and increase distention.
Acute retention is a medical emergency. Waiting an hour lets distention and pain get worse.
Correct. Sudden painful inability to void with a firm, dull bladder suggests acute retention after anesthesia. A bladder scan quickly confirms the volume so decompression can proceed without delay.
questions.rationale: Anesthesia is a major risk factor for urinary retention. Sudden painful inability to void despite a full bladder, a firm distended bladder, and dullness on percussion are the manifestations of acute retention, a medical emergency. A noninvasive bladder scan confirms the volume and leads to decompression by catheterization. Fluids, waiting, and opioids delay treatment or make retention worse.
questions.takeaway: Sudden painful inability to void with a firm, dull bladder = acute retention, an emergency. Scan, then decompress.
questions.hintContent: Connect anesthesia as a risk factor with the manifestations of acute retention and the noninvasive test that measures bladder volume.
questions.hintStrategy: Recognize the emergency first. Then pick the action that moves fastest toward relief without causing harm.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man is being evaluated for chronic urinary retention. Which findings would the nurse expect? Select all that apply.
options: Difficulty starting the urine stream
Sudden, severe suprapubic pain with no urine output
A weak urine flow
Feeling the urge to void again shortly after voiding
A firm, painful, distended bladder with inability to void
optionRationales: Correct. Hesitancy is a manifestation of chronic retention.
Sudden, severe pain with no output describes acute retention, which is a medical emergency.
Correct. A weak stream is typical of chronic retention, often from an obstructed outlet.
Correct. Because the bladder never fully empties, urgency returns soon after voiding.
A firm, painful, distended bladder with inability to void describes acute retention.
questions.rationale: Acute retention is a sudden, painful inability to void despite a full bladder. Chronic retention is painless: the person urinates but cannot fully empty, so there is difficulty starting or maintaining the stream, a weak flow, frequency, and urgency after voiding. Telling the two apart guides how urgently the nurse acts.
questions.takeaway: Chronic retention = painless, weak stream, hesitancy, frequency, urgency after voiding. Acute = painful and can’t void.
questions.hintContent: Contrast the manifestations of acute and chronic urinary retention.
questions.hintStrategy: Sort each finding: painful and sudden, or painless and ongoing?

questions.stem: A nurse on a medical unit is reviewing clients’ risk for urinary retention. Which clients are at increased risk? Select all that apply.
options: A client who took diphenhydramine (Benadryl) to help her sleep
A client with a fecal impaction
A client taking furosemide (Lasix) twice daily
A 68-year-old man with an enlarged prostate
A client with stress incontinence after childbirth
optionRationales: Correct. Antihistamines, like anticholinergics, reduce detrusor contraction and are listed risk factors for retention.
Correct. A mass of hard stool presses on the bladder neck and urethra. Constipation and impaction are known causes of urinary retention.
Diuretics increase urine volume and are a risk factor for incontinence, not retention.
Correct. An enlarged prostate narrows the urethra and blocks outflow.
Stress incontinence comes from low urethral resistance. It causes leakage, not retention.
questions.rationale: Risk factors for retention either block the outlet (enlarged prostate, kidney stones, impacted stool) or weaken the push from the detrusor (anticholinergics, antihistamines, anesthesia, nerve injury, poor detrusor tone). Diuretics and weak urethral resistance lead to leakage instead.
questions.takeaway: Retention = blocked outlet or weak detrusor. Antihistamines, impaction, and an enlarged prostate all qualify.
questions.hintContent: Recall the risk factors for urinary retention and how a full rectum affects the bladder.
questions.hintStrategy: For each client, ask whether the factor blocks outflow or weakens bladder contraction, or instead causes leakage.

tabs.html: Client reports feeling like the bladder is “never empty” and needing to go again right after voiding. Lower abdomen rounded above pubis. Bladder scan after void: 600 mL. Vital signs stable; mucous membranes moist.

questions.stem: A 70-kg client is 1 day post-op. The nurse reviews the 8-hour shift data in the exhibit. Which interpretation is most accurate?
options: The kidneys are producing urine, but the bladder is retaining it, so voided output is well below the expected 280 mL
The client is dehydrated, so IV fluids should be increased to raise urine output
Voided output is low, which signals kidney failure, so the provider should be told the kidneys have stopped filtering
Output is adequate because the client has voided twice during the shift
optionRationales: Correct. The expected output is 0.5 mL/kg/hr × 70 kg × 8 hr = 280 mL. Only 100 mL was voided, yet the scan shows 600 mL retained. Small, frequent voids with a large residual mean retention.
Intake was 1,400 mL and membranes are moist, and 600 mL is sitting in the bladder. The client is not dehydrated, and more fluid would worsen distention.
The 600 mL in the bladder shows urine is being produced. The problem is emptying, not kidney filtering.
The number of voids does not show adequacy. 100 mL in 8 hours is far below expected, and most of the urine is retained.
questions.rationale: Applying 0.5 mL/kg/hr gives an expected 280 mL for 8 hours. Voided output alone (100 mL) looks like oliguria, but the bladder scan shows 600 mL retained. With a feeling of incomplete emptying and urgency after voiding, this is retention after anesthesia. Output looks low only because urine is not leaving the bladder. The plan is bladder decompression, not more fluid.
questions.takeaway: Low voided output plus a large post-void residual = retention, not kidney failure. Always compare with 0.5 mL/kg/hr.
questions.hintContent: Apply the expected urine output formula. Connect the bladder scan result and the reported symptoms to whether the problem is producing urine or emptying it.
questions.hintStrategy: Calculate the expected output, then ask where the missing urine is. Is it not being made, or not getting out?

questions.stem: A client with chronic urinary retention has an indwelling catheter. For the past 2 hours there has been no urine in the drainage bag, and the client reports suprapubic fullness and an urge to void. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Notify the provider that the client may be developing acute kidney failure
Check the tubing for kinks or dependent loops and the bag’s position
Remove the catheter and ask the client to try to void
Encourage the client to drink more fluids to flush the catheter
optionRationales: Suprapubic fullness means urine is being made and is collecting in the bladder. Kidney failure is not the likely explanation, and checking the system comes first.
Correct. No drainage with a full bladder suggests a mechanical obstruction. Kinks, a client lying on the tubing, or a bag above the bladder are quick, common causes the nurse can fix right away.
Removing a catheter requires an order. A client with known retention likely could not void and would become more distended.
More fluid adds to a bladder that is not draining. The flow problem has to be found first.
questions.rationale: When urine collects in the bladder but not in the bag, the drainage system is the first suspect. The nurse checks for kinks, tubing compression, dependent loops, and bag position before assuming kidney failure or changing the catheter. Catheter care is part of reducing retention and preventing UTIs.
questions.takeaway: Catheter not draining and the bladder is full? Check the tubing and bag position first.
questions.hintContent: Connect suprapubic fullness to where the urine is. Recall basic indwelling catheter care and drainage principles.
questions.hintStrategy: Rule out the simplest, most fixable cause before choosing invasive or provider-level actions.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man is having trouble voiding on post-op day 1. His activity order allows him out of bed with assistance, and the provider has prescribed the Credé maneuver if needed. Which nursing actions promote voiding? Select all that apply.
options: Help him stand at the bedside to use the urinal
Turn on the water in the sink while he tries to void
Close the door and curtain and step out of the room
Ask him to finish quickly because transport is on the way
Encourage him to wait until the urge is very strong so he empties more
Apply gentle downward pressure over his lower abdomen as prescribed
optionRationales: Correct. A typical voiding position (standing for most men) uses gravity and intra-abdominal pressure to help empty the bladder.
Correct. Sensory stimuli such as running water help him relax and trigger the urge.
Correct. Privacy promotes relaxation of the urinary sphincter.
Rushing him prevents relaxation. Clients need enough time to void.
Delaying voiding overstretches the bladder. Timely help to the toilet prevents delays.
Correct. The Credé maneuver uses manual pressure over the bladder to help decompress it and reduce retention.
questions.rationale: Normal voiding is promoted through positioning (a typical position that uses intra-abdominal pressure), relaxation (privacy, enough time, sensory stimuli), and timing (no delays). The Credé maneuver is listed as a way to reduce retention by decompressing the bladder.
questions.takeaway: Promote voiding with position, privacy, time, running water, and no delays. Use the Credé maneuver when prescribed.
questions.hintContent: Recall the measures for maintaining normal voiding habits and the ways to reduce urinary retention.
questions.hintStrategy: Ask whether each action helps the client relax and use normal positioning, or adds stress or delay.

questions.stem: A client with urinary retention from poor detrusor muscle tone is started on bethanechol (Urecholine). Which finding best shows that the medication is having its intended effect?
options: The client reports fewer sudden, strong urges to void each day
The client’s urine has turned a reddish-orange color
The client voids 350 mL with a post-void residual of 50 mL
The client reports fewer painful bladder spasms since starting it
optionRationales: Fewer urges is the goal of anticholinergic therapy for urge incontinence, not of a cholinergic drug given for retention.
Reddish-orange urine is an expected effect of phenazopyridine (Pyridium), a urinary analgesic.
Correct. Bethanechol is a cholinergic that promotes urination. A good void with a small residual shows the bladder is now emptying.
Fewer bladder spasms is the goal of urinary antispasmodics.
questions.rationale: Cholinergic medications such as bethanechol stimulate the detrusor to contract and promote urination, so they are used for retention. Effectiveness is shown by better emptying: adequate voided volume and a small post-void residual. The other options describe the goals of different drug classes.
questions.takeaway: Bethanechol (cholinergic) promotes urination. It is working when the client voids well with a low residual.
questions.hintContent: Contrast cholinergic and anticholinergic urinary drugs. Recall how bladder emptying is measured.
questions.hintStrategy: Identify what the drug is supposed to do, then choose the measurable finding that shows it happened.

questions.stem: A nurse receives report on four clients. Which client should the nurse see first?
options: A 75-year-old man with BPH who reports a weak stream and the urge to void again right after he finishes voiding
A client 2 days postpartum who is voiding 300 to 400 mL at a time
A client with an indwelling catheter draining 45 mL/hr of clear yellow urine
A post-op client who has not voided in 9 hours, is restless, and has a firm, tender, distended bladder
optionRationales: A weak stream and urgency after voiding describe chronic retention. It is painless and needs follow-up, but it is not urgent.
Urine output increases early after delivery. Voids of 300 to 400 mL show she is emptying well.
45 mL/hr is above the 30 mL/hr average and the 0.5 mL/kg/hr expectation. The catheter is draining well.
Correct. No voiding for 9 hours with restlessness and a firm, tender, distended bladder after surgery means acute retention, a medical emergency that needs decompression.
questions.rationale: Acute urinary retention, a sudden painful inability to void with a distended bladder, is a medical emergency. Chronic retention is painless and is managed over time. Adequate postpartum voids and a well-draining catheter are expected findings.
questions.takeaway: Acute painful retention comes before chronic retention and stable output.
questions.hintContent: Compare acute and chronic retention. Recall normal urine output values and the expected postpartum changes.
questions.hintStrategy: Identify the one client with a sudden, painful change that could cause harm if not treated now.

questions.stem: A nurse is identifying clients at risk for urinary retention related to lifespan factors. Which clients have a risk factor? Select all that apply.
options: A 6-year-old boy with a congenital narrowing of the urethra
A woman 12 hours after a cesarean birth
A 4-year-old who voids 6 to 8 times a day
A woman with scarring from genital cutting in childhood
A 20-year-old who drinks 2.5 L of fluid a day
optionRationales: Correct. Physical or congenital deformities are a risk factor for retention in children.
Correct. Cesarean delivery, birth trauma, and urogynecologic surgery increase retention risk.
Voiding 6 to 8 times a day is a normal pattern for a child.
Correct. Genital mutilation can cause infection and scarring that obstruct urine flow.
Adequate fluid intake is not a retention risk.
questions.rationale: Lifespan risk factors for retention include congenital deformities and scarring from circumcision complications or genital mutilation in children. In pregnancy they include cesarean delivery, birth trauma, and urogynecology surgery. Normal voiding patterns and adequate fluid are not risks.
questions.takeaway: Lifespan retention risks: congenital deformity or scarring in children; cesarean, birth trauma, or urogynecology surgery in women.
questions.hintContent: Recall the lifespan considerations listed for urinary retention.
questions.hintStrategy: Judge each client on whether the factor can obstruct flow or impair bladder emptying.

questions.stem: An 80-year-old resident who has not had a bowel movement in 7 days now voids only small amounts and has a distended lower abdomen. A digital exam reveals a hard mass of stool in the rectum. Which explanation best links these findings?
options: The hard stool mass presses on the bladder neck and urethra and blocks urine flow
Weeks of straining have permanently weakened the detrusor muscle
Constipation causes dehydration, so the kidneys have stopped making urine
Bacteria from the stool have caused a UTI, which is the only reason for the small voids
optionRationales: Correct. Fecal impaction causes urinary retention. The packed rectum compresses the bladder outlet, so small voids and a distended abdomen follow.
Straining is not described as permanently weakening the detrusor, and the findings came on with the impaction.
A distended lower abdomen suggests urine is being retained, not that the kidneys have stopped making it.
Repeated UTIs are a retention risk factor, but nothing here suggests infection. The impaction explains the findings directly.
questions.rationale: Hardened stool collecting in the rectum raises pressure in the colon and causes urinary retention by compressing the bladder neck and urethra. Constipation is also a listed risk factor for both retention and incontinence. Relieving the impaction is part of relieving the retention.
questions.takeaway: Fecal impaction can cause urinary retention. Check the bowels when a client can’t empty the bladder.
questions.hintContent: Connect the pathophysiology of fecal impaction with the risk factors for urinary retention.
questions.hintStrategy: Choose the explanation that ties together both findings in the stem without adding information that isn’t there.

questions.stem: A nurse suspects fecal impaction in an 86-year-old resident who has had no formed stool for 6 days. Which findings support this suspicion? Select all that apply.
options: Small amounts of liquid, foul-smelling stool leaking onto the brief
Rectal pain with repeated urges that produce nothing
A soft, formed stool each morning
Abdominal distention and cramping with nausea
An increased appetite over the past few days
optionRationales: Correct. Liquid, foul-smelling material seeps around the impaction when there is no formed stool. This is often mistaken for diarrhea.
Correct. Rectal pain and nonproductive attempts to defecate are manifestations of impaction.
A daily soft, formed stool shows normal elimination and argues against impaction.
Correct. Abdominal distention, cramping, and nausea or vomiting occur with impaction.
Clients with impaction are usually anorexic. An increased appetite does not fit.
questions.rationale: Fecal impaction is a mass of hardened stool in the rectum or colon. It shows up as liquid, foul-smelling stool seeping around the mass without formed stool, rectal pain, nonproductive straining, anorexia, abdominal distention, cramping, and nausea or vomiting.
questions.takeaway: Liquid seepage with no formed stool in a constipated client = suspect impaction, not diarrhea.
questions.hintContent: Recall the clinical manifestations of fecal impaction, especially the seepage pattern.
questions.hintStrategy: For each finding, ask whether it fits a hard mass blocking the rectum or fits normal or improved elimination.

questions.stem: Assistive personnel report that an 88-year-old resident “has had diarrhea for 2 days,” with small, liquid, foul-smelling stools on her brief. Her record shows no formed stool for 7 days, and she takes oxycodone and ferrous sulfate daily. She has a PRN order for loperamide (an antidiarrheal). Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Give the PRN loperamide to slow the liquid stools
Assess her abdomen and perform a digital rectal exam per protocol
Hold the oxycodone and ferrous sulfate until the provider can be reached
Teach her to increase her fluid and fiber intake
optionRationales: Giving an antidiarrheal on the assumption of diarrhea could worsen an impaction. Leakage around hard stool is not true diarrhea.
Correct. Seven days without formed stool, constipating medications, and liquid seepage suggest impaction. Abdominal assessment and a digital rectal exam confirm it before treatment.
These medications contribute to constipation, but holding prescribed drugs is not the first step and needs a provider decision.
Fluid and fiber help prevent constipation but will not resolve an existing impaction. This teaching comes later.
questions.rationale: Liquid, foul-smelling stool with no formed stool is a classic sign of fecal impaction: liquid seeps around the hard mass. Opioids and iron are constipating. The nurse assesses first (abdomen, bowel sounds, digital rectal exam) rather than treating a mislabeled ‘diarrhea’ with an antidiarrheal.
questions.takeaway: ‘Diarrhea’ in a constipated client on opioids or iron? Assess for impaction before giving an antidiarrheal.
questions.hintContent: Connect the seepage sign, constipating medications, and the assessment techniques for bowel elimination.
questions.hintStrategy: Question the label the report gives you. Assess to confirm the real problem before you treat it.

questions.stem: During digital removal of a fecal impaction, the client becomes pale and lightheaded. The heart rate drops from 78/min to 46/min, and the blood pressure falls from 128/76 to 92/54 mm Hg. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Finish removing the stool quickly so the stimulation ends sooner
Give the prescribed oil-retention enema to soften the remaining stool
Stop the procedure and monitor the client’s vital signs
Raise the head of the bed and continue more slowly
optionRationales: Continuing keeps stimulating the vagus nerve and can worsen the bradycardia and hypotension.
An enema follows successful manual removal. Giving it now ignores an unstable client and adds rectal stimulation.
Correct. Bradycardia, hypotension, and pallor during manual removal signal a vasovagal response. Stopping removes the stimulus, and close monitoring tracks recovery.
Any continued rectal stimulation keeps the vagal response going. The procedure must stop.
questions.rationale: Manual removal breaks the impaction into smaller pieces, followed by an enema or suppository. Rectal stimulation can trigger a vasovagal response with bradycardia, hypotension, and lightheadedness. The nurse monitors for this throughout, and if it occurs, stops immediately and assesses vital signs.
questions.takeaway: Manual disimpaction: watch for a vasovagal response (low HR and BP). If it happens, stop.
questions.hintContent: Recall the procedure for manual removal of an impaction and the complication to monitor for.
questions.hintStrategy: Identify the physiologic response from the vital signs. Then remove its cause.

questions.stem: A 79-year-old client reports hard stools and straining for a month. The nurse reviews her medication list. Which medications are likely contributing to her constipation? Select all that apply.
options: Oxycodone 5 mg every 6 hours as needed for back pain
Ferrous sulfate 325 mg daily for anemia
Polyethylene glycol (MiraLAX) 17 g as needed
Diphenhydramine 25 mg at bedtime for sleep
Docusate (a stool softener) 100 mg twice daily
Psyllium fiber supplement daily
optionRationales: Correct. Opioids slow intestinal motility, which lets more water be absorbed from the stool.
Correct. Iron is a common constipating medication. Prenatal vitamins cause constipation in pregnancy for the same reason.
Polyethylene glycol is a laxative used to treat constipation.
Correct. Antihistamines are on the list of constipating medications.
Stool softeners are used to manage constipation, not cause it.
Fiber adds bulk and is part of preventing and managing constipation.
questions.rationale: Opioids, iron, antihistamines, antacids, and antidepressants are medications that contribute to constipation. Older adults are at higher risk because they take more medications and are often less active. Laxatives, stool softeners, and fiber are treatments.
questions.takeaway: Constipating drugs: opioids, iron, antihistamines, antacids, antidepressants.
questions.hintContent: Recall the medication risk factors for constipation and the drugs used to treat it.
questions.hintStrategy: Sort each medication: does it slow the bowel, or is it given to keep the bowel moving?

questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman with occasional constipation asks how much fiber she should eat and where to get it. Which response by the nurse is accurate?
options: “About 38 grams a day, mostly from cheese, eggs, and lean meats.”
“About 10 grams a day, mostly from white bread and white rice.”
“About 25 grams a day, with less fluid so the extra fiber stays bulky.”
“About 25 grams a day, from whole grains, fruit, and vegetables.”
optionRationales: 38 g is the goal for men, and cheese, eggs, and meat contain little or no fiber.
10 g is far below the goal, and refined grains are low in fiber.
25 g is the right amount, but fiber needs adequate fluid to work. Reducing fluid can worsen constipation.
Correct. The goal for women is 25 g a day, from whole-grain cereals and breads, fresh fruit, and vegetables, with adequate fluid.
questions.rationale: Dietary management of constipation sets fiber goals of 25 g a day for women and 38 g a day for men. Fiber comes from whole-grain cereals and breads, fresh fruit, and vegetables, together with adequate fluid. Fiber without fluid can harden stool.
questions.takeaway: Fiber: 25 g/day for women, 38 g/day for men, from whole grains, fruit, and vegetables, plus fluid.
questions.hintContent: Recall the daily fiber targets by sex and the high-fiber food sources.
questions.hintStrategy: Check each option for both the right number for this client and the right food sources and fluid advice.

questions.stem: A client reports that for the past 4 months she has had about two bowel movements a week, strains with most of them, and passes hard, lumpy stools. She has not used laxatives. How should the nurse interpret these findings?
options: They meet chronic constipation criteria: two or more symptoms for at least 12 weeks
They are not constipation, because she still has a bowel movement every single week
They suggest acute constipation that should resolve with one dose of a laxative
They indicate fecal impaction, because her stools are hard
optionRationales: Correct. Rome IV criteria for chronic constipation require two or more of: straining, lumpy or hard stool, a feeling of incomplete emptying, manual maneuvers, or fewer than 3 BMs a week, for at least 12 weeks. She has three of these for 16 weeks.
Constipation is defined by fewer than 3 bowel movements a week or difficult passage, not by having none.
Four months of symptoms is chronic, not acute, and a single laxative dose is not the management approach.
Impaction is a mass of hardened stool with seepage of liquid and nonproductive straining. She is still passing stool.
questions.rationale: Constipation means fewer than 3 BMs a week or difficult passage of hard, dry stools. Chronic constipation by Rome IV criteria is two or more of: straining, lumpy or hard stool, incomplete emptying, manual maneuvers, or fewer than 3 BMs a week, lasting at least 12 weeks. This client has straining, hard stools, and 2 BMs a week for 4 months.
questions.takeaway: Chronic constipation = 2 or more Rome IV criteria for at least 12 weeks.
questions.hintContent: Recall the definition of constipation and the Rome IV criteria for chronic constipation.
questions.hintStrategy: Count how many criteria she meets and for how long. Compare with the required number and duration.

questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: A 78-year-old client takes a stimulant laxative every night because “I’ve got to have a bowel movement every day.” After teaching, which statements by the client indicate understanding? Select all that apply.
options: “It’s okay not to go every day as long as my stools are soft and easy to pass.”
“Using laxatives every night can make my bowels stop working on their own.”
“I’ll drink less water so I don’t have to get up at night to urinate.”
“If I have belly pain and haven’t gone in days, I’ll take an extra laxative.”
“A walk every day will help my bowels move.”
“I’ll sit on the toilet after breakfast when I feel the urge instead of putting it off.”
optionRationales: Correct. Older adults often have perceived constipation, the belief that a daily BM is required. Normal frequency varies.
Correct. Chronic laxative use interferes with normal bowel reflexes and can cause constipation rather than relieve it.
Older adults often limit fluid because of urinary incontinence or reduced thirst, which hardens stool. Fluid should not be limited.
Laxatives should not be used when there may be a blockage. Pain with no BM for days should be reported.
Correct. Physical activity promotes motility, and decreased activity is a risk factor in older adults.
Correct. Responding to the urge, especially after meals (the gastrocolic reflex), is part of behavior management. Ignoring the urge is a risk factor.
questions.rationale: Risk factors in older adults include decreased activity, more medications, poor dentition, little fresh produce, self-limited fluid intake, and perceived constipation. Prevention includes fiber, fluid, exercise, responding to the urge, and avoiding overuse of laxatives, which blunt normal bowel reflexes.
questions.takeaway: Older adults: a daily BM isn’t required. Laxative overuse backfires, and they shouldn’t limit fluids.
questions.hintContent: Recall the lifespan factors for constipation in older adults and the prevention measures.
questions.hintStrategy: Check each statement against the prevention list. Watch for fluid restriction and for laxative use when a blockage is possible.

questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: A client at 28 weeks’ gestation reports hard stools every 3 to 4 days and new hemorrhoids. She asks why this is happening. Which explanation by the nurse is most accurate?
options: “The baby absorbs most of the fluid you drink, so your stool dries out and hardens.”
“Higher progesterone slows your bowel, the uterus crowds it, and iron adds to it.”
“Constipation in pregnancy usually means your intestine is partly blocked.”
“Your prenatal vitamin is the only cause, so you should stop taking it.”
optionRationales: This is not the mechanism. Maternal fluid intake and stool hydration are not explained by the fetus absorbing fluid.
Correct. Increased progesterone slows peristalsis, the growing uterus displaces the small intestine, and prenatal iron is constipating. Hemorrhoids often follow.
Constipation in pregnancy is common and expected. It does not usually signal obstruction.
Iron contributes, but it is one of several causes. Stopping a prescribed prenatal vitamin is not appropriate.
questions.rationale: In pregnancy, increased progesterone slows motility, the growing uterus displaces the intestines, and prenatal iron is constipating. Straining with hard stools contributes to hemorrhoids. Management uses fiber, fluids, and activity rather than stopping prenatal vitamins.
questions.takeaway: Pregnancy constipation = progesterone + crowding by the uterus + iron.
questions.hintContent: Recall the lifespan factors for constipation during pregnancy.
questions.hintStrategy: Choose the answer that names all the contributing causes accurately without advising a harmful change.

questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: The parent of a 6-year-old who has been toilet trained since age 3 says that for the past 6 weeks the child has had only one bowel movement a week. The stools are large, hard, and painful, sometimes clog the toilet, and the child hides to hold them in. Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?
options: “He is holding it in on purpose, so taking away privileges after accidents will help.”
“Constipation can’t be diagnosed until age 8, so it’s best to watch and wait for now.”
“A set toilet time after meals, more fiber, fluids, and activity will help.”
“A daily enema until his stools are normal will retrain his bowel quickly.”
optionRationales: Punishment adds stress and fear, which makes withholding worse. Painful stools lead to holding them in.
Constipation is diagnosed in children older than 4. This child meets the criteria.

Correct. Children’s constipation is managed with behavior modification, a scheduled toilet routine, diet, regular activity, and a laxative if needed. Softer stools make defecation less painful, so withholding decreases.
Daily enemas are invasive and are not the first-line intervention. Behavior and diet changes come first.
questions.rationale: Constipation in children older than 4 is diagnosed by symptoms lasting a month after toilet training: fewer than 2 stools a week, painful hard BMs, large-diameter stools that clog the toilet, a large rectal mass, and excessive voluntary withholding. Pain causes withholding, and withholding causes harder stools. Interventions are behavior modification, scheduled toileting, diet, activity, and a laxative if needed.
questions.takeaway: Children’s constipation: painful stools lead to withholding. Break the cycle with routine, diet, and activity, not punishment.
questions.hintContent: Recall the diagnostic criteria and interventions for constipation in children, including the psychologic influence of pain.
questions.hintStrategy: Check the age criterion first. Then choose the least invasive approach that addresses the cause.

questions.stem: A client has not had a bowel movement in 6 days. This afternoon the client has worsening abdominal distention and cramping, has vomited twice, and is not passing flatus. Bowel sounds are hypoactive. The client has a PRN order for polyethylene glycol (MiraLAX). Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Give the polyethylene glycol with a full glass of water
Encourage the client to walk in the hallway to stimulate peristalsis
Offer a high-fiber snack and warm fluids to promote a bowel movement
Withhold the laxative and notify the provider of these findings
optionRationales: Laxatives should not be used when there is a blockage or obstruction. These findings suggest one.
Activity helps prevent constipation, but it does not address a possible obstruction. Delaying the report is unsafe.
Adding food and fiber to a possibly obstructed bowel can increase distention and vomiting.

Correct. Vomiting, increasing distention, no flatus, and hypoactive bowel sounds after days without a BM suggest obstruction. Laxatives are contraindicated, and the provider needs to evaluate the client.
questions.rationale: Impaction and obstruction raise pressure in the colon and can lead to ulceration, perforation, and reduced perfusion. Laxatives are contraindicated with a blockage or obstruction. When constipation progresses to vomiting, no flatus, and distention, the nurse holds bowel stimulants and reports promptly.
questions.takeaway: No laxatives with a suspected blockage. Vomiting, distention, and no flatus mean report it.
questions.hintContent: Connect the signs of a possible bowel obstruction to the contraindications for laxatives.
questions.hintStrategy: Ask whether the usual constipation treatment is safe with these new findings.
