questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A nurse is teaching a group of new assistive personnel about the effects of an untreated fecal impaction. Which statements about these effects are accurate? Select all that apply.
options: Increased pressure in the colon can lead to ulceration or perforation
The mass can press on the bladder outlet and cause urinary retention
The longer the stool stays in the colon, the softer it becomes
Liquid stool can leak around the mass and be mistaken for diarrhea
Impaction increases urine production through the kidneys
The anal sphincter muscle becomes stronger from holding the mass
optionRationales: Correct. A retained mass raises pressure in the colon and can reduce perfusion of the bowel wall, causing ulceration and perforation.
Correct. Impaction can compress the bladder neck and urethra and cause urinary retention.
Water keeps being removed from retained stool, so it becomes harder, sometimes as hard as concrete.
Correct. Liquid seeps around the impaction, which can look like diarrhea or fecal incontinence.
Impaction affects bladder emptying, not urine production by the kidneys.
Impaction does not strengthen the anal sphincter. It stretches the rectum and causes seepage.
questions.rationale: In impaction, retained stool keeps losing water and hardens. Pressure in the colon can cause ulceration, perforation, and reduced perfusion. The mass can cause urinary retention, and liquid stool seeping around it can be mistaken for diarrhea or incontinence.
questions.takeaway: Impaction hardens over time and can cause perforation, urinary retention, and seepage that looks like diarrhea.
questions.hintContent: Recall the pathophysiology of constipation and impaction: water absorption, colon pressure, and effects on nearby organs.
questions.hintStrategy: For each statement, ask what a hard, enlarging mass that keeps losing water would do to the colon and nearby structures.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Exemplar: Bowel Incontinence, Constipation & Impaction · Constipation & Fecal Impaction
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A client on bed rest receiving opioids for pain asks why his stools have become so hard and dry. Which explanation by the nurse is accurate?
options: “When stool moves slowly, the colon has more time to absorb water from it.”
“Bed rest speeds up the bowel, so stool passes before it can form.”
“The pain medicine makes the bowel secrete extra mucus, which dries the stool.”
“Hard stool is caused by too much fluid in your diet.”
optionRationales: Correct. Opioids and immobility slow transit, and slower movement allows more fluid absorption, so stools become dry and hard.
Immobility slows motility. It does not speed it up.
Opioids slow motility. Extra mucus is not why stools become hard.
Adequate fluid softens stool. Low fluid intake contributes to hard stools.
questions.rationale: Constipation develops when slow-moving stool loses more water to the colon. Immobility and opioids both slow motility, which is why they are listed risk factors. Activity, fluid, and fiber counteract this.
questions.takeaway: Slower transit means more water absorbed, which means harder stool.
questions.hintContent: Recall the pathophysiology of constipation and the effects of immobility and opioids on motility.
questions.hintStrategy: Think about what happens to stool water when transit time increases.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Exemplar: Bowel Incontinence, Constipation & Impaction · Constipation & Fecal Impaction
questions.clientNeed: Psychosocial Integrity
questions.stem: A 7-year-old is brought to the clinic for recurrent soiling at school. The child has hard, painful bowel movements, says, “I’m too busy to go,” and has become withdrawn. While assessing the abdomen, the nurse notices several bruises in different stages of healing on the child’s back and upper arms. Which action is the priority?
options: Teach the parent to add fiber and a scheduled toilet time after meals
Document the bruises and report suspected abuse as required
Recommend a meeting with the child’s teacher about bathroom access
Explain to the parent that encopresis is usually caused by stubbornness
optionRationales: Fiber and scheduled toileting are part of encopresis therapy, but child safety comes first.
Correct. Encopresis therapy includes considering abuse. Bruises in different stages of healing with emotional withdrawal are red flags that the nurse must document and report.
Working with teachers is part of the plan, but it does not address the possible abuse.
Encopresis involves constipation, withholding, stress, and emotional factors. Blaming the child is inaccurate and not therapeutic.
questions.rationale: Encopresis is recurrent soiling in a child who should have bowel control. It is linked to constipation, withholding, small hard painful BMs, emotional withdrawal, and stress. Therapy includes family education, psychological support, fiber, behavior management, working with teachers, and considering abuse. Signs of possible abuse take priority over the bowel plan.
questions.takeaway: Encopresis: always consider abuse. Safety comes before the bowel plan.
questions.hintContent: Recall the manifestations and therapy of encopresis, including the safety consideration listed.
questions.hintStrategy: Several options are part of the long-term plan. Ask which finding threatens the child’s safety right now.

questions.clientNeed: Psychosocial Integrity
questions.stem: A 72-year-old client admitted for pneumonia denies any bowel problems. Which observations should prompt the nurse to assess further for fecal incontinence? Select all that apply.
options: Asks to go to the bathroom many times each hour
A faint fecal odor and stained underwear
One soft, formed bowel movement each morning
Seems distracted and anxious during the interview
Bowel sounds present in all four quadrants
optionRationales: Correct. Frequent requests for bathroom breaks can be a way of managing incontinence the client hasn’t disclosed.
Correct. Fecal odor and soiled clothing are observable cues to incontinence.
A daily soft, formed stool is a normal pattern.
Correct. Distraction and anxiety may reflect embarrassment and fear of an accident, so the nurse should explore further.
Bowel sounds in all quadrants are a normal finding.
questions.rationale: Fecal incontinence is emotionally distressing, and clients often don’t report it. Observation picks up cues: frequent bathroom requests, fecal odor, soiled clothing, and distraction or anxiety. The interview then explores extent, onset, and duration.
questions.takeaway: Clients often hide fecal incontinence. Watch for frequent bathroom trips, odor, soiling, and anxiety.
questions.hintContent: Recall the observation and interview cues in the nursing assessment of fecal incontinence.
questions.hintStrategy: Separate behaviors and signs that suggest hidden incontinence from findings that are simply normal.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A client reports being unable to hold back gas and having minor staining of underwear, but can control formed stool. How should the nurse classify this?
options: Major fecal incontinence
Fecal impaction with seepage
Partial fecal incontinence
Encopresis
optionRationales: Major fecal incontinence is the inability to control feces of normal consistency.
Impaction is a mass of hardened stool with liquid seepage. It is not described here.
Correct. Partial fecal incontinence is the inability to control flatus or prevent minor soiling.
Encopresis is recurrent soiling in a child who should have bowel control.
questions.rationale: Fecal incontinence is the loss of voluntary control of fecal or gaseous matter. Partial incontinence means the person cannot control flatus or prevent minor soiling. Major incontinence means the person cannot control normal-consistency stool.
questions.takeaway: Partial = gas and minor soiling. Major = can’t control normal stool.
questions.hintContent: Recall the definitions of partial and major fecal incontinence.
questions.hintStrategy: Ask whether the client can control normal stool. That separates partial from major.

questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: A nurse is screening clients at a community health fair. Which factors increase a client’s risk for fecal incontinence? Select all that apply.
options: Smoking one pack of cigarettes a day
Walking 30 minutes most days
A BMI of 36
Male sex
Dementia
A diet high in fiber
optionRationales: Correct. Smoking is a listed risk factor for fecal incontinence.
Regular physical activity is a prevention measure.
Correct. Being overweight or obese raises risk.
Female sex, not male sex, is the listed risk factor.
Correct. Confusion and dementia interfere with recognizing and responding to the urge to defecate.
Fiber is a prevention measure because it promotes formed, controllable stool.
questions.rationale: Risk factors for fecal incontinence include advanced age, female sex, smoking, and a high BMI. Causes include neurologic problems (spinal cord injury), trauma, inflammation, infection, and physiologic problems (depression, confusion, dementia). Prevention is physical activity, fiber, fluid, Kegels, avoiding straining, and treating the underlying cause. Fecal incontinence is not a normal change of aging.
questions.takeaway: Fecal incontinence risks: older age, female, smoking, high BMI, dementia. Activity and fiber prevent it.
questions.hintContent: Recall the etiology, risk factors, and prevention of fecal incontinence.
questions.hintStrategy: Sort each factor as a risk or as a prevention measure.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
questions.stem: A long-term care resident with major fecal incontinence has had several loose stools today. The perineal skin is red and moist, with one small open area. Which intervention is the priority?
options: Apply an absorbent brief and check it for soiling every 4 hours
Limit her fluids to reduce the volume and frequency of stool
Teach her Kegel exercises to improve her anal sphincter control
Cleanse gently after each episode and apply a moisture barrier
optionRationales: Leaving stool against the skin for up to 4 hours worsens the breakdown already present.
Loose stools already cause fluid loss. Restricting fluid risks dehydration.
Kegels may help long-term prevention, but they do nothing for the skin breakdown happening now.
Correct. Liquid stool is very irritating. Prompt, gentle cleansing and a barrier protect skin that is already breaking down.
questions.rationale: Impaired skin integrity is on the problem list for fecal incontinence, and diarrhea adds fluid loss and a high risk of skin breakdown. With an open area already present, the priority is prompt cleansing and barrier protection. Perineal hygiene is a planned outcome.
questions.takeaway: Incontinence plus loose stool: clean promptly and protect the skin. Don’t limit fluids.
questions.hintContent: Connect diarrhea and fecal incontinence to skin breakdown risk and the problem list.
questions.hintStrategy: Look for the actual injury in the stem. Then choose the action that stops it from getting worse.

questions.clientNeed: Psychosocial Integrity
questions.stem: A 70-year-old client with partial fecal incontinence tells the nurse, “I’ve stopped going to my grandson’s ball games. What if I have an accident in the stands?” Which nursing response best addresses the client’s concern?
options: “Let’s plan for game days: toilet first, find restrooms, and pack supplies.”
“Many people your age have this, since it’s a normal part of getting older.”
“It might be best to stay home until your bowel control gets better.”
“A colostomy would end the accidents, so you should ask your surgeon about one.”
optionRationales: Correct. A planned outcome is identifying strategies to maintain social interactions. Practical planning lowers the fear of an accident.
Fecal incontinence is not a normal change of aging. Normalizing it dismisses the concern and the chance for treatment.
Staying home deepens the social isolation that fecal incontinence often causes.
Surgery is an option for some clients, but jumping to a colostomy skips first-line management and doesn’t address the concern now.
questions.rationale: Fecal incontinence is emotionally distressing and often leads to social isolation and low self-esteem. Patient-centered planning includes strategies to keep up social interactions, along with the bowel regimen and perineal hygiene.
questions.takeaway: Fecal incontinence leads to isolation. Plan strategies that keep the client socially active.
questions.hintContent: Recall the psychosocial effects of fecal incontinence and the planned outcomes in the nursing process.
questions.hintStrategy: Choose the response that keeps the client involved and gives practical help, not one that dismisses or withdraws.

questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care
questions.stem: Two weeks ago, a client with chronic constipation and fecal incontinence from overflow agreed to the goal “soft, formed stool three times per week.” Her log shows only one hard stool a week and two episodes of soiling. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Request a prescription for a daily stimulant laxative
Ask about her fluids, fiber, activity, and obstacles to the plan
Revise the goal to one soft stool per week so it is achievable
Document that the goal was partly met and continue the plan unchanged
optionRationales: Adding a laxative changes the plan before the nurse knows why it failed. Prolonged laxative use is also discouraged.
Correct. The nurse explores why the goals were not met (diet, fluids, activity, obstacles, and whether education and support were enough) before changing the plan.
Lowering the goal before finding the cause accepts a poor outcome without solving anything.
The goal was not met. Continuing unchanged ignores the evaluation data.
questions.rationale: Evaluation in the bowel nursing process asks whether bowel habits improved, whether fluid and diet are adequate, whether activity is adequate, what obstacles exist, and whether education and support were enough. Reasons goals are not met are explored before the plan is modified.
questions.takeaway: Goal not met? Explore why before you change the plan.
questions.hintContent: Recall the evaluation step of the nursing process for bowel elimination.
questions.hintStrategy: All the options change or continue the plan. Pick the one that gathers the information needed to decide how.

questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care
questions.stem: A nurse is writing outcomes for a client with constipation and fecal incontinence. Which outcome statement is written correctly?
options: The client will understand the importance of dietary fiber
The nurse will teach the client about high-fiber foods before discharge
The client will list four foods high in fiber by discharge
The client will have normal bowel habits
optionRationales: ‘Understand’ cannot be observed or measured.
This describes a nursing action, not a client outcome.
Correct. It is client-centered, observable, measurable, and time-limited. Listing 4 high-fiber foods is one of the planned outcomes.
‘Normal bowel habits’ is vague and has no criteria or time frame.
questions.rationale: Planning uses patient-centered, measurable outcomes, such as a soft, formed BM within 4 hours of a laxative, a soft, formed stool 3 times a week, or listing 4 high-fiber foods. Good outcomes name the client, an observable behavior, criteria, and a time frame.
questions.takeaway: Outcomes: client-centered, observable, measurable, and timed (for example, lists 4 high-fiber foods by discharge).
questions.hintContent: Recall the planning outcomes listed for bowel elimination and what makes an outcome measurable.
questions.hintStrategy: Eliminate options that describe nurse actions or use words you can’t observe.

questions.stem: A nurse teaches a 65-year-old woman how to prevent fecal incontinence. Which statements by the client indicate that teaching was effective? Select all that apply.
options: “I’ll do my pelvic floor squeezes every day.”
“I’ll drink less so my stools aren’t as loose.”
“I’ll try not to strain when I have a bowel movement.”
“I’ll wait until it’s convenient instead of going right when I feel the urge.”
“I’ll take a laxative every day to keep my bowels empty.”
optionRationales: Correct. Kegel exercises strengthen the pelvic floor, which supports both bladder and rectal control.
Fluid is part of prevention. Limiting it hardens stool and leads to constipation and straining.
Correct. Avoiding straining protects the pelvic floor and anal sphincter.
Ignoring the urge leads to constipation and overflow soiling.
Daily laxatives interfere with normal bowel reflexes and can cause loose stools that are harder to control.
questions.rationale: Fecal incontinence prevention includes regular physical activity, fiber, fluid, Kegel exercises, avoiding straining, and treating underlying causes such as infection. The same pelvic floor exercises used for urinary incontinence improve rectal muscle tone.
questions.takeaway: Prevent fecal incontinence with activity, fiber, fluid, Kegels, and no straining.
questions.hintContent: Recall the prevention measures for fecal incontinence and how Kegels affect the rectum.
questions.hintStrategy: Check each statement against the prevention list. Reject fluid limits, ignoring the urge, and laxative overuse.

questions.stem: A client with fecal incontinence from an anal sphincter injury during childbirth asks about surgery. Which procedure repairs the anal sphincter?
options: Colostomy
Transurethral resection of the prostate
Cystocele repair
Anal sphincteroplasty
optionRationales: A colostomy diverts stool through the abdominal wall. It is a surgical option, but it does not repair the sphincter.
TURP removes prostate tissue in men with BPH.
A cystocele repair corrects a prolapsed bladder in urinary incontinence.
Correct. Anal sphincteroplasty repairs the anal sphincter to treat fecal incontinence.
questions.rationale: Surgical options related to fecal incontinence include anal sphincteroplasty, which repairs the sphincter, and colostomy, which diverts stool. TURP and cystocele repair treat urinary problems.
questions.takeaway: Sphincteroplasty repairs the sphincter. A colostomy diverts stool.
questions.hintContent: Recall the surgical options for fecal incontinence and those for urinary incontinence.
questions.hintStrategy: Match the procedure to the structure it repairs.
